thread.title_full: Crockett Park Volunteers Clean Babb Cemetery - NewsBreak

author: Tim Massey
title: Crockett Park Volunteers Clean Babb Cemetery - NewsBreak
text:
By Tim Massey ,
4 hours ago
True to the Crockett spirit the staff and volunteers of David Crockett Birthplace State Park have reached out offering service to the community. While they have been busy themselves at the park following Helein’s devastation, serving the greater community is a part of their mission.
In a joint project with the Greene County Heritage Trust, and its America 250 project committee, members of the Crockett Friends group, and descendants of the Babb, Crockett and Hawkins families, the park staff endeavored to remove brush blocking accessibility to the Seth Babb Family Cemetery. In addition to restoring visitor accessibility the group cleaned the historic headstones. A new sign was added as the old one had become weathered and unreadable.
The cemetery area was last cleared by members of the Sons of the American Revolution in 2016 for a grave marking service. Ben Stonecyfer and his wife have kept the cemetery mowed since then, but it was the outlying area that had become overgrown with downed trees preventing access.
Park manager Joe Nowatarski said, “The headstone cleaner was applied and will take time to work its magic, but for now, a new sign was installed, the driveway cleared, a parking area mowed, and respects were paid.”
According to the Babb Family Association, “The Babb Farm Cemetery is located across the street from the original location of the 1787 Seth Babb Homestead near the town of Chucky about 9 miles north of Greeneville, TN. The cemetery needs constant maintenance to protect and preserve the grounds.
It is home to Seth Babb and Annie Stonecipher and their families. The Homestead that Seth built now stands about 1 block from the courthouse in Greenville and is on display and is adjacent to the Homestead of our 17th President, Andrew Johnson.”
The Babb Home is maintained by the Greeneville Greene County History Museum in Fox park. It is open during museum hours for visitors.
Seith Babb served in the American Revolution from the state of Virginia and was at the Battle of Yorktown in 1781 which was the last major battle of the revolution. A marker at his grave says he saw General Washington and Lord Cornwallis after the surrender.
Also in the cemetery is Joseph Hawkins, the uncle of David Crockett. Hawkins, born 1753, served in the 2nd Virginia State Regiment, which joined the Continental Army at Valley Forge for the winter of 1777-78. He served from March 1778 through November 1779, also participating in the Battle of Monmouth in New Jersey.
In his autobiography Crockett wrote: “While I was still a small child, Joseph Hawkins, who was a brother to my mother, was hunting in the woods for deer. He was passing near a thicket of brush, in which one of our neighbors was gathering some grapes, as it was in the fall of the year, and grape season. The body of the man was hid by the brush, and it was only as he would raise his hand to pull the bunches, that any part of him could be seen. It was a likely place for a deer; and my uncle, having no suspicion that it was any human being, but supposing the raising of the hand to be the occasional twitch of a deer’s ear, fired at the lump, and as the devil would have it, unfortunately shot the man through his body.
I saw my father draw a silk handkerchief through the bullet hole, and entirely through his body; yet after a while he got well, as little as anyone would have thought. What become of him, or whether he is dead or alive, I don’t know; but I reckon he didn’t fancy the business of gathering grapes in an out-of-the-way thicket soon again.” The man who was shot through the body was Absalom Stonecipher.
Henry Stenecypher, another veteran of the Revolutionary war is nearby. He served at the Battle of Cowpens and Guilford Courthouse under Col. Benjamin Cleveland.
Also nearby is William Hunt, a veteran of the Civil War. Many of the stones are now unreadable, many are just fieldstones, but each has a story to tell and each deserves our respect.
There is some unique grave markers here identified as a stone cross monument or a medieval wayside cross. With their circular tops these often symbolize the cycle of life.
The Babb Cemetery is a lovely spot to visit and offers a bench for those that would like to sit and meditate. Thanks to the crew from the David Crockett Birthplace, the space is now accessible for visitors to enjoy.
Nowotarski reminded readers, to “Please consider driving out to visit Babb Farm Cemetery to preserve history and celebrate America’s 250.”

Ben Stonecyfer and his wife have kept the cemetery mowed since then, but it was the outlying area that had become overgrown with downed trees preventing access.
